blocks.title: An Introduction to Environment and Environmental Studies
Protecting Our Environment: Policies and Practices

topics.name: Global Issues: Climate, Ozone, Acid Rain & Disasters
topics.summary: The greenhouse effect and climate change with the treaties and India's action plan, ozone depletion, acid rain, and natural disasters.
points: Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, ozone, CFCs, water vapour) trap outgoing infrared heat and keep the earth at about +15°C instead of −18°C. Water vapour causes about two-thirds of the effect and CO₂ about a quarter; nitrogen, oxygen and argon do not absorb infrared. Sulphur dioxide is not a greenhouse gas.
Of incoming solar radiation, about a third is reflected, about 20% is absorbed by atmospheric gases and the rest by the surface.
Global warming effects: sea-level rise (warming water expands and ice melts), more floods and droughts, farm and forest losses, and more malaria, dengue and yellow fever.

Climate treaties: the IPCC was set up in 1988 by WMO and UNEP; UNFCCC was adopted at Rio in 1992 and came into force in 1994; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) required developed countries to cut greenhouse gases 5.2% below 1990 levels; the Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015) aims to keep warming well below 2°C.

India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) has 8 missions: solar, enhanced energy efficiency, sustainable habitat, water, sustaining the Himalayan ecosystem, Green India, sustainable agriculture, and strategic knowledge for climate change.

The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere (15–50 km), is measured in Dobson units and absorbs about 99% of UV. UVA is least energetic and not absorbed; most UVB is absorbed (2–3% reaches us) and causes skin cancer and cataract; UVC is absorbed by oxygen and ozone.

CFCs (used in sprays, deodorants, paints, refrigeration) are stable, rise to the stratosphere, and are broken by UV, releasing chlorine that destroys ozone. The Vienna Convention (1985) led to the Montreal Protocol (16 September 1987) — 16 September is Ozone Day.

Acid rain comes from sulphur and nitrogen oxides (not CFCs). Unpolluted rain has a pH of about 5.7; precipitation below 5.7 counts as acid deposition. It harms crops, forests, aquatic life and buildings, and causes heart and lung problems.

Disaster types: atmospheric (heat waves, cyclones — which form over tropical seas warmer than about 27°C), geological (earthquakes, landslides, avalanches), hydrological (floods, drought) and biological (pest invasions). Asia is the region most prone to natural calamities.

Tsunamis are seismic sea waves; the Indian coast's most devastating one was in 2004, and mangroves are a natural defence. Zone V is India's most severe seismic zone (very high damage risk); the Rann of Kachchh is in a high zone.
mistakes: Confusing the Montreal Protocol (ozone) with the Kyoto Protocol (greenhouse gases).
examples:
Example: the greenhouse effect in a parked car
A car left in the sun with its windows shut gets much hotter inside than outside: sunlight enters through the glass, but the heat given off inside cannot escape easily. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour do the same for the earth — keeping it at about +15°C rather than −18°C. Adding more of them traps more heat and causes global warming.

Examples: ozone, acid rain and disasters in India
Ozone: CFCs from old refrigerators and sprays drift up to the stratosphere, where UV light frees chlorine that breaks down ozone — the reason the Montreal Protocol phased CFCs out.
Acid rain: sulphur dioxide from industry around Agra was linked to the yellowing of the Taj Mahal's marble, leading to the Taj Trapezium case.
Disasters: in the 2004 tsunami, stretches of the Tamil Nadu coast behind dense mangroves suffered less damage — mangroves act as a natural barrier.

topics.name: Biodiversity & Its Conservation
topics.summary: Levels and values of biodiversity, India's biogeographic zones and hotspots, threats to biodiversity, and in-situ and ex-situ conservation.
points: 'Biological diversity' was coined by Thomas Lovejoy (1980) and 'biodiversity' by E.O. Wilson. Levels: genetic diversity (the 'fundamental currency of diversity', e.g. varieties of mango or rice), species diversity (the most visible) and ecosystem diversity.

About 12.5 million species are estimated and 1.7 million described. In sheer numbers, insects and micro-organisms are the most abundant; insects are the largest described group (about 960,000 species).
India's 10 biogeographic zones: Trans-Himalaya (e.g. Ladakh), Himalaya, Indian Desert, Semi-arid, Western Ghats, Deccan Peninsula (the largest), Gangetic Plain, North-East, Islands and Coasts.

Zone facts: the Thar's wildlife is known for extraordinary adaptations (desert fox, desert cat, Houbara bustard); the Western Ghats hold about two-thirds of India's endemic plants (lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr, Malabar grey hornbill, spiny dormouse); the rhinoceros is found only in the Brahmaputra valley.

Hotspots: areas extremely rich in species, with high endemism and under constant threat (Myers, 1988). There are 34 worldwide; 4 are in India and its neighbours. Tropical rain forests and coral reefs hold the most species.
India is mega-diverse: 4 hotspots, 26 endemism centres, 2 realms, 3 biomes, 10 biogeographic zones, about 33% of recorded flora endemic, and one of 12 centres of origin of cultivated plants.
Values: direct use (food, timber); indirect use (non-consumptive, aesthetic, cultural and religious, ethical); non-use (option, bequest, existence).
Threats: habitat loss (the greatest), invasive species, over-hunting, pollution and climate change. Fragile habitats: coral reefs, oceanic islands, mountain tops and habitat islands.

Examples: the passenger pigeon was wiped out by selective destruction for food; rinderpest from cattle held back the Great Indian Rhinoceros; DDT and other chlorinated pesticides cut bird numbers such as the bald eagle; commercial hunting targets tiger, snow leopard and cheetah skins, elephant ivory, rhino horn and whales.

Invasive species: water hyacinth (harms fish and rice), Parthenium or Congress weed (skin allergies), Prosopis juliflora or mesquite (semi-arid areas), golden apple snail. Climate change is likely to worsen the problem.

In-situ conservation: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, wetlands, tiger and elephant reserves. Ex-situ: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks ('genetic insurance'), tissue culture, captive breeding, artificial insemination (elephants, cheetahs, black-footed ferret) and fostering (whooping crane, peregrine falcon).

Biosphere reserves come from UNESCO's MAB (Man and the Biosphere) programme; each has a core, a buffer (regulated use such as grazing and farming, no hunting) and a transition zone. India's first was Nilgiri. Mangroves act as a natural bulwark against sea erosion; Chilika and Bharatpur were India's first Ramsar wetlands.
examples:
Example: the three levels of biodiversity
Genetic: India has grown thousands of rice varieties, each with different traits such as drought or flood tolerance.
Species: the Western Ghats hold endemic species like the lion-tailed macaque and the Nilgiri tahr.
Ecosystem: the Sundarbans mangroves, the Thar desert and the Himalayan forests are very different ecosystems within one country.

Example: in-situ vs ex-situ, and an invasive species
In-situ: the one-horned rhinoceros is protected in its own habitat in Kaziranga National Park.
Ex-situ: seeds of crop varieties are stored in seed banks as 'genetic insurance', and endangered animals are bred in zoos for release.
Invasive: water hyacinth spreads over lakes and backwaters, blocking sunlight and boats and harming fish.

topics.name: Pollution & Waste Management
topics.summary: Types of pollutants, air, water, soil and noise pollution with their standards and tests, and how hazardous and solid waste is minimised, treated and disposed of.
points: Primary pollutants are emitted directly (sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, hydrocarbons, particulates); secondary pollutants form in the air (ozone, PAN, nitric acid, sulphuric acid, sulphur trioxide, smog). Smog is not a natural pollutant; pollen and volcanic gases are.

Point sources discharge at one place (chimneys, pipes); non-point sources are spread out (runoff from farms). Biodegradable pollutants (paper) break down; persistent ones (pesticides, heavy metals, plastics, rubber) do not.
Bioaccumulation is a pollutant entering and building up in an organism; biomagnification is its concentration rising from one link of the food chain to the next.

Air: particles smaller than 10 µm (PM10) are respirable suspended particulate matter (RSPM), with a standard of 60 µg per cubic metre; PM2.5 goes deep into the lungs. Radon (from building materials) and formaldehyde are indoor pollutants.

Water pollutants are biological (pathogens), chemical (inorganic, organic and radioactive substances) or physical (suspended and settled solids, heat). Phosphates and nitrates cause eutrophication; sewage uses up oxygen in water.
Water tests: MPN detects coliforms such as E. coli; BOD is the oxygen bacteria use to break down organic matter (high BOD means low dissolved oxygen); TDS is total dissolved solids.
Noise is measured in decibels; dB(A) accounts for both pressure and pitch. The prescribed night-time limit for residential areas is 45 dB(A). The Bhopal gas tragedy released methyl isocyanate.
Hazardous waste strategy: minimise → recycle → treat → dispose. Minimisation methods: process modification, waste concentration, waste segregation (recycling is a separate step).

Treatment — physical: phase separation (lagooning, tank storage, sludge drying beds); chemical: oxidation, reduction, neutralisation, heavy-metal precipitation, oil–water separation; sludge processing (biological): conditioning, digestion, composting, thickening or dewatering, solidification.

Disposal — landfill (sanitary landfills are lined with clay or plastic); incineration, used where land is short and excellent for minimising and detoxifying waste but very costly if the heat is not reused (hospital waste is incinerated); dumping at sea; underground disposal, the option for radioactive nuclear waste.
mistakes: Lagooning is a physical treatment (phase separation); conditioning is part of sludge processing — past papers test this both ways.
examples:
Example: biomagnification of DDT
In a classic study, DDT was about 0.000003 ppm in the water, 0.04 ppm in zooplankton, 0.5 ppm in small fish, 2 ppm in large fish and about 25 ppm in fish-eating birds. The concentration rises at each step of the food chain, so top predators suffer most — birds laid thin-shelled eggs that broke.

Examples: primary vs secondary pollutants, and BOD
Car exhaust releases nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons (primary). In sunlight they react to form ozone and PAN (secondary) — the brown photochemical smog seen over busy cities.
When untreated sewage enters a river, bacteria use up oxygen to break it down. BOD rises, dissolved oxygen falls, and fish die.

topics.name: Natural Resources: Water, Land & Energy
topics.summary: Water and its cycle, soils and land conservation, forests and deforestation, and conventional and non-conventional energy.
points: Oceans hold 97% of the earth's water; less than 3% is fresh. Of fresh water about 80% is frozen and about 20% liquid (mostly groundwater). Only about 1% of all water is readily usable; agriculture takes about 70% of what is used.

Water cycle terms: runoff is the main source of water for lakes and rivers; sublimation is ice turning straight into vapour; transpiration is water vapour lost from plants. An aquifer is a layer of rock that water percolates into and is held in.

Traditional water systems: johads, kuls (channels carrying glacier water to villages in Spiti, Himachal Pradesh) and bamboo drip irrigation (North-East). Sprinkler irrigation is modern. Too much irrigation causes waterlogging, salinity or alkalinity and lower yields.
Floods are the most common calamity; Bangladesh and India together account for over two-thirds of flood deaths. Economic impacts of drought: loss of crops, dairy, livestock and fish.

Soils as the IGNOU book describes them: red — potatoes, bananas, pineapples, rubber; black (Deccan and Malwa plateaux) — cotton, sugarcane, groundnut, soyabean; desert — low organic matter and fertility; Himalayan — low fertility; alluvial — Indo-Gangetic plains.

Soil care: gypsum treats alkaline soil; manure improves soil cohesion, water retention and structure (not salinity). Erosion is controlled by plant cover, drainage, check dams, stone walls along coasts and tree barriers; ravines (e.g. Chambal) come from gully erosion. Finer particles in sewage settle with alum and caustic soda.

Forest functions: economic (timber, food, medicines, products used as insecticides and pesticides), ecological (moderating climate as a carbon sink, protecting biodiversity, checking erosion, landslides, cyclones and floods, cleaning air, protecting watersheds) and socio-cultural. India needs 33% of its area under forest.

Four major causes of deforestation: population explosion, forest fires, grazing and pest attacks. Crown fires occur in dense forests. NTFPs are items like medicinal herbs, edible flowers, leaves and fruits (timber and firewood are separate).
Joint Forest Management began informally in 1972 in Midnapore, West Bengal. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 gives rights to tribal and other forest dwellers.
Energy sources — conventional: coal, oil, natural gas, hydropower, atomic energy; non-conventional: solar, wind, biomass, geothermal, fuel cells (best fuel: hydrogen), co-generation, wave and tidal.

India's energy: coal meets over half of energy needs and 63% of commercial energy; natural gas about 7%; biomass is the most used in rural India. China is the largest coal producer; Bombay High produces the most oil; the first wave energy plant was at Vizhinjam, Kerala; geothermal potential is in the North-West Himalaya.

Sludge gas, like biogas, is mostly methane; a biomass gasifier turns solid fuel into gas; photovoltaic cells turn sunlight into electricity. With development, growth in per-capita energy demand slows in the industrial sector but keeps rising in transport, residential and commercial sectors.
mistakes: IGNOU's book lists rubber under red soil — laterite soil is not described in it.
examples:
Example: how little water we can use
Imagine all the earth's water as 100 litres. About 97 litres are sea water; under 3 litres are fresh. Of that fresh water, about 80% is locked in ice, and most of the rest is underground. Less than a litre is easy to use — which is why saving and recharging water matter.

Example: a village biogas plant
Cow dung and kitchen waste are fed into a digester; bacteria break them down without air to produce biogas, which is mostly methane, for cooking. The leftover slurry is a good manure. The village cuts firewood use (saving forests) and smoke in kitchens — a non-conventional, renewable source of energy.

topics.name: Ecosystem Structure, Energy Flow & Cycles
topics.summary: What an ecosystem is, its living and non-living parts, trophic levels and food chains, energy flow, nutrient cycles and ecological succession.
points: An ecosystem is the basic functional unit of nature: organisms interacting with each other and with their physical surroundings. It has no fixed size or boundary and regulates itself through feedback. The term was coined by Tansley.

Biosphere: the zone of land (lithosphere), water (hydrosphere) and air (atmosphere) where life exists — from about 11,000 m below the ocean surface to about 9,000 m above mean sea level. Life is abundant from about 200 m below sea level to about 6,000 m above.

Abiotic components: light, temperature, rainfall, water, nutrients. Biotic: producers (autotrophs), consumers (heterotrophs or phagotrophs) and decomposers (saprotrophs or reducers — mainly bacteria and fungi). Chemosynthetic bacteria are autotrophs.

Trophic levels: I producers → II herbivores (primary consumers) → III carnivores (secondary) → IV tertiary consumers → V top carnivores (quaternary). Tigers, lions and vultures are top carnivores; humans, as omnivores, sit at several levels.
Food chains: grazing (starts with green plants), detritus (starts with dead, decaying organic matter) and parasitic (e.g. goat → nematodes → bacteria). Linked food chains form a food web.
Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is lost as heat at each level, so ecosystems are open systems that need a constant input of solar energy. The sun also drives the water cycle.

Nutrient cycles are gaseous (reservoir: atmosphere or hydrosphere — water, carbon, nitrogen) or sedimentary (reservoir: earth's crust — phosphorus, calcium). The sulphur cycle is mostly sedimentary with a short gaseous phase; its large reservoir is soil and sediments. Nitrogen's main reservoir is the atmosphere.

Ecological succession: lichens form the pioneer community on bare rock, followed by mosses, grasses, shrubs and trees. Each intermediate stage is a sere (seral stage); the final, stable stage is the climax community.
Primary succession starts on an area that never had life; secondary succession follows the destruction of an existing community.
examples:
Example: a pond as an ecosystem
Abiotic: water, sunlight, dissolved oxygen and nutrients. Producers: phytoplankton and water plants. Primary consumers: zooplankton and small fish that eat them. Secondary consumers: larger fish. Top consumers: kingfishers. Decomposers: bacteria and fungi on the bottom, returning nutrients to the water.
Food chain: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish → kingfisher.

Example: energy loss and succession
Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next: 10,000 units in plants → 1,000 in herbivores → 100 in carnivores → 10 in top carnivores. This is why food chains are short and top predators are few.
On a bare rock, lichens come first, then mosses, grasses, shrubs and finally trees — primary succession ending in a climax forest.

topics.name: Forest, Grassland, Desert & Aquatic Ecosystems
topics.summary: The main forest types and their plants and animals, grasslands, deserts and their adaptations, and freshwater, marine and estuarine ecosystems.
points: Coniferous (boreal, taiga) forest: spruce, fir and pine; cold, long winters; soil acidic and poor in minerals; the lowest productivity of any ecosystem.
Temperate deciduous forest: broad-leaved trees that shed leaves in winter; trees 40–50 m tall with thin, broad leaves — maple, beech, oak, hickory; rainfall 75–150 cm.

Temperate evergreen forest (Mediterranean-type climate): low evergreen trees such as hemlock, yew and maple; shrubs up to 3–4 m. Temperate rain forest: the coldest rainforest, where fog can matter more than rain.

Tropical rain forest: near the equator, over 200 cm rain a year, the most diverse forest — under 7% of the land but over 50% of known species (about 62% of known plants). Animals include chameleons, agamids, geckos, ant-eaters, giant flying squirrels and sloths.
Tropical seasonal (monsoon) forest: teak and bamboo, as in central India. Subtropical rain forest: epiphytes, vines and strangler fig.
Grasslands get about 25–75 cm of rain; in Indian grasslands biomass peaks around September–October. Deserts get under 25 cm.

Desert adaptations: some nocturnal rodents pass very concentrated urine and never need to drink. In the Thar, the lizards Calotes and Uromastyx prey on the desert locust, and the main predatory birds are vultures (e.g. white-rumped vulture, Gyps bengalensis).
Freshwater ecosystems are lentic (standing — lakes, ponds, impoundments, wetlands) or lotic (flowing — rivers, streams). Rivers are open (heterotrophic) systems; lakes are closed.
Aquatic organisms: plankton drift; neuston live unattached at the air–water surface; periphyton are attached to stems and leaves of rooted plants; nekton swim; benthos live on the bottom.

Ocean zones: littoral (shore — the most variable in temperature, light, salinity and moisture), neritic (shallow coastal — rich in species and highly productive), pelagic (open sea, 90% of the ocean surface), benthic (floor). Sea water averages about 3.5% salt.

Estuary: the transition zone between river and sea, with unique ecological features and biotic communities. Estuaries are brackish, the most productive ecosystems and nurseries for fish (e.g. Kerala coast, Sundarbans). Brackish ecosystems include estuaries, salt marshes and mangroves.
mistakes: Hemlock, yew and maple are listed under temperate evergreen forest; maple, beech and oak under temperate deciduous.
examples:
Examples: aquatic ecosystems
Lentic (standing water): a lake or pond. Lotic (flowing water): a river or stream.
Estuary: where a river meets the sea, as in the Sundarbans — brackish, very productive, and a nursery for fish and prawns.
Nekton (fish that swim), plankton (drifting algae and tiny animals) and benthos (crabs and worms on the bottom) live at different levels of the same water body.

Example: living in a desert
Desert animals save water: many rodents stay in burrows by day and come out at night, and some produce very concentrated urine and hardly ever drink. Desert plants have thick, waxy stems and spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss.

topics.name: Environment, Population & Sustainable Development
topics.summary: What the environment is, its three types, how thinkers see the human–environment link, sustainable development and the SDGs, and human population growth.
points: Environment: the sum total of living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components, influences and events around an organism.

Three types in the IGNOU book — natural: oceans, rivers, lakes, forests, grasslands, deserts; human-modified: orchards, plantations, sanctuaries, parks; human-made: cities, towns, industries, crop fields, dams, artificial lakes.
Determinism (nature controls humans): developed by Friedrich Ratzel and expanded by Ellsworth Huntington. Possibilism (humans choose among what nature allows): the term was coined by Lucien Febvre.

Sustainable development: meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs — defined by the Brundtland Commission (WCED, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland) in 'Our Common Future'. Herman Daly called the term an 'oxymoron'.

Transitions a sustainable society needs include a demographic transition (growing → stable population), a resource transition and a technological transition (pollution-intensive → environment-friendly production).

Priority areas for sustainable development: slow population growth; reduce poverty, inequality and Third World debt; make agriculture sustainable; protect forests and habitats; use water and energy sustainably; reduce waste. 'Zero pollution' is not one of them.

SDGs: 17 goals for 2016–2030 — e.g. no poverty, zero hunger, good health and well-being, quality education, gender equality, clean water and sanitation, affordable and clean energy, climate action, life below water, life on land. Past-paper distractors that are not SDGs: tourism, clean air, life on air, quality health care, social equity.

Population history: about 5 million people at the dawn of agriculture (about 8000 BC); growth up to about 1800 AD came with agriculture; in the 14th century the bubonic plague killed more than half the population of Europe and Asia.
Projected world population: 8.6 billion (mid-2030s), 9.8 billion (mid-2050s) and 11.2 billion by 2100.

Carrying capacity: biophysical = the maximum population the planet's resources can support at a given level of technology; social = the sustainable number within a society's patterns of consumption and trade, always lower. It varies with resource availability, culture and level of economic development.
mistakes: Crop fields and dams are human-made in the IGNOU book, not human-modified; orchards, plantations and sanctuaries are human-modified.
examples:
Example: three types of environment in one district
Natural: a forest and a river. Human-modified: a rubber plantation and a wildlife sanctuary. Human-made: the town, a dam and the industrial estate.

Example: sustainable development in practice
A fishing community agrees not to fish during the breeding season and to use nets with larger holes so young fish escape. Catches may be smaller now, but fish stocks remain for their children — meeting present needs without harming future generations (the Brundtland idea). Clean water, clean energy and life below water are among the SDGs this supports.

topics.name: Environmental Laws, Institutions & Constitution
topics.summary: The Constitution's environment clauses, Indian environmental Acts with their years, the NGT and NBA, international conventions and ENVIS.
points: The 42nd Amendment (1976), made after the 1972 Stockholm conference, added Article 48A (the State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife) and Article 51A(g) (a fundamental duty of every citizen).
The Department of Environment began in 1980, became the Ministry of Environment and Forests in 1985, and was renamed the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in 2014.

Acts: Indian Forest Act 1927; Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 (Schedules I–V); Water Act 1974 (amended 1988); Water Cess Act 1977; Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; Air Act 1981; Environment (Protection) Act 1986 — the 'umbrella' law passed after Bhopal.
The 1987 amendment of the Air Act strengthened enforcement, introduced stiffer penalties and citizen suits, and brought in noise pollution.
The Biodiversity Bill (introduced 2000, passed 2002) set up the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), which has the powers of a civil court and deals with access by foreigners.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT Act 2010, set up October 2010) exists for the effective and speedy disposal of environmental cases, aiming to decide them within 6 months. Principal bench: New Delhi; zonal benches: Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai.
Species projects: Hangul (1970), Lion (1972), Tiger (1973), Crocodile (1974), Brown-antlered deer (1981), Elephant (1991–92). There is no camel project.

International milestones: Stockholm 1972 (gave rise to UNEP); CITES 1973; Vienna 1985 (ozone); Montreal Protocol 1987; Basel 1989 (movement of hazardous waste across borders); Rio Earth Summit 1992 (Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD); Kyoto 1997; Rotterdam 1998 (hazardous chemicals); Stockholm 2001 (persistent organic pollutants); Johannesburg 2002 (Rio+10); Ramsar 1971 (wetlands).

ENVIS is the environmental information system of the Environment Ministry, with its main centre in Delhi. Centres include CPCB (pollution control), ITRC Lucknow (toxic chemicals), TERI (renewable energy and environment), NIOH Ahmedabad (occupational health) and CTS, IISc Bengaluru (Western Ghats ecology). TIFR and AIIMS are not ENVIS centres.
Laws are hard to enforce because of a lack of expertise, shortage of funds and a lack of seriousness among implementing authorities.
mistakes: Mixing up Act years — make a one-line list and revise it on exam day.
examples:
Examples: which law or body applies?
A factory releases untreated effluent into a river → Water Act 1974, enforced by the pollution control boards.
Someone kills a tiger → Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 (the tiger is in Schedule I, the highest protection).
A company wants to clear forest land for a mine → Forest (Conservation) Act 1980: it needs the Central Government's approval.
Residents want speedy relief against a polluting unit → they can approach the National Green Tribunal.

topics.name: Environmental Movements, Ethics & Justice
topics.summary: The three views of nature, attitudes towards nature, why we need environmental ethics, equity, justice and racism, and India's environmental movements.
points: Three views of nature: Western (European and North American) — nature is alien and hostile, to be conquered; Sinaitic (Chinese, Korean, Japanese) — nature is beautiful and humans are part of it; Indian (Hindu, Buddhist and Jain) — nature is a mother and a goddess who cannot be tamed.

Attitudes: anthropocentrism puts far greater value on humans than on anything else; stewardship is a strong sense of responsibility for a particular part of nature — strong in tribal, pastoral and traditional farming communities, weak in urban ones.

Ecofeminism was proposed as an alternative to patriarchal systems of domination. Biocentrism holds that all living organisms have values and rights whether or not they are useful; ecocentrism extends rights to ecosystems and non-living parts of nature. Aldo Leopold wrote the essay 'The Land Ethic'.
A new set of environmental ethics is needed because of new effects on nature, new knowledge about nature and expanding moral concerns.

Environmental equity has three categories: procedural (unfair procedures — packing boards with business interests, holding hearings in remote places, English-only material for non-English speakers); geographical (communities hosting waste sites get fewer benefits than those producing the waste); social (decisions that mirror power and racial bias, e.g. against certain ethnic groups).

Environmental justice means equal protection under environmental laws for everyone regardless of race, ethnicity or income; environmental racism is the placing of hazards on disadvantaged communities.
Religions teach us to be trustees or stewards of the environment, not its masters. Environmental education and organised collective action (student groups, campaigns) change attitudes.

Movements and cases: Chipko (Chandi Prasad Bhatt), Silent Valley (the valley of the Kunthi river, Kerala), Narmada Bachao Andolan, and the Taj Trapezium case (Agra's brick kilns, the Mathura refinery and Firozabad's glass factories).
examples:
Example: Chipko and Silent Valley
Chipko (1970s, Garhwal Himalaya): when contractors came to fell trees, village women, led at Reni by Gaura Devi, hugged the trees to protect them. Their protest led to a ban on commercial felling in the area.
Silent Valley (Kerala): a proposed hydroelectric dam on the Kunthi river would have flooded rare rain forest. After a long campaign by scientists and citizens, the project was dropped and the area became a national park.

Example: environmental inequity
A city's garbage comes mostly from well-off areas, but the dump is placed next to a poor settlement — geographical inequity. If the public hearing on it is held far away and only in English, that is procedural inequity too.

topics.name: Environment & Human Health
topics.summary: Health and public health, the genetic, behavioural and environmental influences on health, and the vocabulary of disease.
points: WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.

Environmental health is the part of public health concerned with all external conditions that affect health. Public health as a discipline began in Europe after 1842 ('the great sanitary awakening') and is now called community health: the patient represents the community.
Aetiology is the study of the cause or origin of disease; the host is the organism a parasite enters and the pathogen is the parasite that causes disease.
Health depends on genetic, behavioural and environmental influences.

Hereditary (genetic) diseases: phenylketonuria, haemophilia, mongolism (Down's syndrome), sickle-cell anaemia, thalassaemia. Allergies, diabetes, hypertension and schizophrenia are not entirely genetic — they come from genes interacting with the environment. Malaria is infectious, not genetic.
Behavioural influences: smoking, alcoholism, drugs, chewing tobacco and irregular eating.

Environmental influences — physical: radiation, noise, vibration, humidity; chemical: poisons and toxins; biological: microbes, animals, allergens; sociological: overcrowding, isolation, neglect; psychological: stress, anxiety, depression, boredom.
examples:
Examples: environmental influences on health
Physical: long exposure to traffic noise causes stress and hearing loss. Chemical: arsenic in groundwater in parts of West Bengal causes skin lesions and cancer. Biological: stagnant water breeds mosquitoes that spread malaria and dengue. Sociological: overcrowded slums spread tuberculosis. Psychological: constant work stress leads to anxiety and depression.

Example: genes vs environment
Thalassaemia and haemophilia are hereditary — passed on through genes. Type 2 diabetes and hypertension come from genes interacting with lifestyle and environment: an inactive life, unhealthy food and stress raise the risk even in people with a family history.

Centre for Theoretical Studies (CTS) Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru
All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi
